title: Laws of UX: Hick's Law (with examples!)
summary: A product designer walks through Hick's law (decision time grows with the number and complexity of choices) and ties it to working-memory limits, then shows practical ways to cut choices: simplified remotes, step-by-step onboarding, a highlighted recommended plan, multi-step forms, Google's one-field home page and category-based settings. He closes with the opposite failure: collapsing options into bare, ambiguous icons that users cannot decode.

insights.insight: Working memory is a small buffer; when new information arrives and the slots are full, something already there gets dropped, often the user's original intention. Every extra option or line of text on a screen competes for those few slots.
insights.visual: Slide 'User's Working Memory': a row of memory slots, three filled, with five incoming items pushing the oldest one out (shown in red).

insights.insight: Modern TV remotes kept only the crucial buttons and moved the rest of the complexity onto the screen, shown only when needed. Keep the always-visible controls to the essential few and surface the rest in context.
insights.visual: Side-by-side photo of an old button-covered remote and a minimal modern remote with a handful of buttons.

insights.insight: When a choice is unavoidable, highlight the recommended option so the decision becomes 'accept or change' instead of 'compare everything'. A visually emphasised default removes most of the deliberation.
insights.visual: A pricing page with three plans where the middle 'Pro' plan is raised and coloured as the recommended one.

insights.insight: A long form shown all at once scares people off; the same fields split into short numbered steps with one Next button feel light. Chunk long input into a few steps, each with a single clear action.
insights.visual: Slide 'Forms': on the left (Bad) a tall grid of fields, on the right (Good) a short 'Step 1' with a few fields and a green Next button.

insights.insight: Google's home page offers essentially one thing to do; extra tabs, filters and tools appear only after the first search. Make the first screen a single obvious action and reveal power features as the person goes deeper.
insights.quote: allows users to actually just get right into the gist
insights.visual: The Google home page: a centred logo and a single search field on an otherwise empty page.

insights.insight: Over-simplifying backfires: reducing a navigation to bare, abstract icons (grid, power, graph) leaves users guessing what each one means. Fewer choices only help when each remaining choice is instantly understandable.
insights.visual: Slide 'Categorisation that doesn't make sense' marked Bad: a smart-home app whose bottom bar is unlabelled icons.

insights.insight: The fix is simple: put a short label under each icon, as Facebook does even for familiar icons. Labels remove ambiguity at almost no cost in space.
insights.visual: Slide 'Facebook Example' marked Good: a phone with a bottom bar of icons each carrying a text label, magnified.

apply_to_wael: On the 'pick level' and 'pick subject' steps, pre-highlight a recommended choice (e.g. Bac / the most-played subject) with Wael pointing at it, so most students confirm with one tap instead of comparing a grid.
Cap each onboarding screen at one primary action and at most 3-5 large, labelled options; if there are more subjects, show the top few and a quiet 'others' entry.
Split account creation into tiny steps (name, then phone or code), one field per screen in landscape, each with a single big Next, instead of a form page.
On the town map, every building or hotspot gets a short Arabic label next to its icon; never rely on an unlabelled symbol for navigation.
